memories: Finished Moby-Dick tonight. Captain Ahab chased the white whale across every ocean and it cost him everything. Ishmael alone survived to tell it, floating on Queequeg's coffin.
Read Treasure Island in one sitting. Jim Hawkins found the map in Billy Bones' sea chest, and Long John Silver played every side of the crew of the Hispaniola.
Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea again. Captain Nemo showed Professor Aronnax the ruins of Atlantis from the salon of the Nautilus. Jules Verne wrote machines before they existed.
The storm in the Odyssey kept me up. Poseidon wrecked Odysseus within sight of Ithaca, and Calypso held him seven years on her island.
Darwin's voyage on the Beagle: five years, and the finches of the Galapagos quietly rewrote everything we thought about living things.
Robinson Crusoe counted his days on the island with notches on a post. Twenty-eight years, and the footprint in the sand still frightened him more than the solitude.
Gulliver woke tied down by threads in Lilliput. Jonathan Swift disguised a whole critique of empires as a sailor's tall tale.
Two Years Before the Mast, Richard Henry Dana's log of rounding Cape Horn as a common sailor. The frozen rigging, the hides on the California coast, the honesty of it.
Galileo's Starry Messenger: he pointed a spyglass at Jupiter in 1610 and found four moons that did not orbit the Earth. Everything tilted from that page on.
Kepler buried in Tycho Brahe's tables for years until the orbits confessed: ellipses, not circles. His third law still feels like music.
Edmond Halley saw that the comets of 1531, 1607 and 1682 were one visitor, and promised it would return in 1758. It did, sixteen years after his death.
William Herschel found Uranus from his garden in Bath in 1781, the first planet discovered since antiquity, with a telescope he ground himself.
Caroline Herschel swept the sky while her brother slept, eight comets to her name and the first woman paid to do science in England.
Tycho Brahe lost his nose in a duel and wore a brass one, but his naked-eye measurements of Mars were precise enough to carry Kepler to the laws.
Copernicus held De Revolutionibus in print only on his deathbed in 1543. He moved the Earth and apologized for it in the preface.
The 1769 transit of Venus: Cook sailed to Tahiti so astronomers could time a black dot crossing the sun and measure the distance to it.
Charles Messier catalogued a hundred smudges so comet hunters would not be fooled. His list of distractions became the map of nebulae and galaxies.
Laplace claimed the solar system needed no further hypothesis to run. Napoleon asked him where God fit, and he answered with mathematics.
Icarus again. Daedalus built the wings and warned him about the sun, and the boy flew high anyway. The sea that took him bears his name.
Prometheus stole fire from Olympus in a fennel stalk and gave it to us. Zeus chained him to a rock in the Caucasus for it, and the eagle came every day.
Orpheus sang his way into the underworld and Hades wept iron tears. One look back at Eurydice at the threshold, and she was gone twice.
Persephone ate six pomegranate seeds in the dark, so Demeter mourns half the year. Winter is a mother missing her daughter.
Theseus followed Ariadne's thread out of the labyrinth after killing the Minotaur, then forgot to change the black sails. Aegeus jumped into his sea.
Pandora opened the jar and every ill flew out into the world. Only hope stayed under the lid, which I have never decided is mercy or cruelty.
The premiere of Beethoven's Ninth, Vienna 1824: he was fully deaf and had to be turned around to see the applause he could not hear.
Bach's Goldberg Variations were written, the story goes, for Count Keyserlingk's sleepless nights. Thirty variations on one aria, and the aria returns at the end unchanged.
Mozart left the Requiem unfinished at the Lacrimosa. Sussmayr stitched the rest from sketches, and nobody fully agrees where one hand ends and the other begins.
Emily Dickinson wrote nearly eighteen hundred poems and published almost none. Hope is the thing with feathers that perches in the soul.
Walt Whitman set Leaves of Grass in type himself in 1855 and kept rewriting it his whole life. I contain multitudes, he said, and meant it as a fact.
Ada Lovelace's notes on Babbage's Analytical Engine, 1843: she saw that a machine for numbers could weave symbols and even music, a century before any computer existed.
